---
title: "Solution: PCA for Dimensionality Reduction and Cluster Visualisation"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)

options(bdat602.source_only = TRUE)
source("courses/bdat-602/_teacher/resources/datasets/simulate_bdat602_data.R")
health_data <- simulate_bdat602(n = 50000, seed = 602)
```

## Task 1: Run prcomp()

```{r task1-prepare}
clust_data <- health_data |>
  select(age, bmi, income, num_claims, num_chronic_conditions) |>
  drop_na() |>
  scale()
```

```{r task1-pca}
pca <- prcomp(clust_data, scale. = FALSE)
summary(pca)
```

## Task 2: Scree plot and variance explained

```{r task2-scree}
pve <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)

tibble(PC = 1:length(pve), PVE = pve, cumPVE = cumsum(pve)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = PVE)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = cumPVE), colour = "red", group = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cumPVE), colour = "red", size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Scree Plot — Insurance Policyholders",
       y = "Proportion of Variance Explained",
       caption = "Red line = cumulative PVE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r task2-80pct}
num_pcs_80 <- min(which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.80))
cat("Number of PCs for 80% variance:", num_pcs_80, "\n")
cat("Cumulative PVE by PC:\n")
round(cumsum(pve), 3)
# Typically PC1 + PC2 explain ~70-80%, and 3 PCs reach ~90%.
```

## Task 3: Biplot — which variables drive PC1 and PC2?

```{r task3-biplot}
biplot(pca, scale = 0, cex = 0.4,
       main = "Biplot — Insurance Policyholder Features")
```

```{r task3-loadings}
round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 3)

# PC1 is most influenced by num_claims and num_chronic_conditions (high positive loadings)
# and age (also positive). PC1 broadly represents "health utilisation and age":
# policyholders with high PC1 scores are older with more conditions and more claims.

# PC2 is most influenced by income (high positive loading) and bmi (negative loading).
# PC2 broadly represents "income vs. health risk": high PC2 = high income, low BMI;
# low PC2 = low income, high BMI.
```

## Task 4: Visualise k-means clusters in PCA space

```{r task4-kmeans}
set.seed(602)
km <- kmeans(clust_data, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
```

```{r task4-scatter}
as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2]) |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(km$cluster)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "k-Means Clusters in PCA Space (PC1 vs PC2)",
       x = "PC1 (Health Utilisation / Age)",
       y = "PC2 (Income vs BMI Risk)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1)))
```

```{r task4-interpret}
# The clusters show reasonable (though not perfect) separation in PC1-PC2 space.
# Some overlap is expected: k-means operates in 5-dimensional space; projecting
# to 2D loses 15-30% of variance depending on the dataset. Two clusters that
# overlap in PC1-PC2 may be separated in PC3 or PC4.
# Additional checks:
# 1. Silhouette scores per cluster (a cluster with low mean silhouette is poorly defined)
# 2. Profile tables (do the cluster means differ meaningfully on key variables?)
# 3. PCA plot in PC1-PC3 or PC2-PC3 space
# Overlap in a 2D PCA plot does NOT mean the clustering has failed.
```
